newsitem.title: UK: Sterling seen resuming uptrend despite sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Sterling seen resuming uptrend despite sell-off.

text.p: Sterling's battering to below 3.0 marks on Tuesday has no doubt cheered exporters but a full-blown trend reversal is unlikely, said analysts.

"The moves we have seen this week are not based on anything solid. The near-term risks are still that rates are going to go up and sterling/mark will test 3.0-3.05 marks," said Mark Geddes, treasury economist at ABN AMRO.
Sterling fell from a high of 3.0627 marks on Monday to a low of 2.9745 marks on Tuesday. At 1320 GMT it was at 2.9760/70.

Against the dollar, which scaled 7-1/2 year peaks just below 1.85 marks on Monday, the pound has skidded from a peak of $1.6640 to six-week lows of $1.6270 on Tuesday. At 1320 GMT it was at 1.6260/50.
Against the mark, however, sterling's sharp decline is barely a dent in a furious rally which has taken sterling up some 35 percent from August 1996 levels around 2.2755 marks.

"I think it is still too early in the day to say that this is a complete change of trend...And that we won't see the pound back above three deutschmarks in the near future," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.

Sterling was battered on Monday, first by a powering dollar which triggered stops and profit-taking and then by the belief in some quarters that UK rates were unlikely to be raised at next week's Bank of England Monetary Policy Committee meeting.
Since May, the BoE has thrice raised interest rates. The UK, with rates of 6.75 percent, boasts some of Europe's meatiest yields.
But a record rise in personal credit in June, suggesting consumers are borrowing and spending freely has turned up the heat for an August rate-rise, said economists.
Technically, moreover, chartists say the pound is shaky but it is not yet in a full-blown trend reversal.
"At this stage, there is not enough evidence to suggest this is the end of the entire upmove," said Ian Stannard, technical analyst at Chase Investment Bank.

"Sterling has been rallying strongly now for around a year, with only a very minor correction in March and May. The fact we have seen a strong pullback is not surprising given the sharp rally," said Stannard.
But Monday's volatile price action has rendered sterling vulnerable.

"After a low at 2.9880, roughly, this one (stg/mark) is bouncing and could see 3.0190 again before the next downleg towards 2.95," said Dominique Corombelle, technical analyst at Generale Bank in Brussels.
Corombelle, however, said the price action in sterling on Monday and Tuesday had succeeded in placing a cap on the pound where the market had previously failed.
"We have the first signal of a reversal, but the confirmation should come with a break of 2.95 marks," said Corombelle.
And while not imminent, economists said the pound's longer-term outlook remained shaky.

"We are in overshoot territory...Which does question sustainability and there is a growing view that later this year, early the next....The economy will slow down quite sharply and that is a sterling negative story," said ABN's Geddes.
